query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting a portion of the heavier Hf content in as-cast HfMoTaTiZr with Al reduces its overall density by several percent while preserving or slightly improving its high-temperature mechanical strength up to approximately 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr high-entropy alloy with high strength from room temperature to ~1000 °C and a density of ~10.21 g cm−3.
generation.intervention: Partial replacement of Hf with ~5–10 at.% Al via vacuum arc melting, followed by high-temperature homogenization.
generation.conditions: Vacuum arc melt the adjusted composition, homogenize at elevated temperature (e.g., ~1200 °C) in an inert environment, then mechanically characterize from room temperature to 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Maintenance of a BCC solid solution (and possibly B2) phase stability while lowering the average atomic mass via Al substitution.
generation.mechanism: Al addition reduces overall density and can stabilize desirable solid-solution or B2 phases that retain high-temperature strength by solid-solution strengthening and minimal formation of brittle intermetallic phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Density decreases by ~5–10% relative to HfMoTaTiZr, while yield strength at ~1000 °C is at least on par with the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr: density = 10.21 g cm−3, high mechanical strength at up to ~1000 °C.
generation.boundary: Performance assessed under compressive or tensile loading from room temperature to ~1000 °C in inert or vacuum atmosphere to avoid oxidation-induced detrimental effects.
generation.uncertainty: If Al amounts or thermal treatments are not carefully optimized, unwanted intermetallics may form, potentially reducing high-temperature ductility and strength.

falsification_experiment.design: Vacuum arc melt a set of alloys with increasing Al content (0–10 at.% Al as Hf replacement), homogenize at ~1200 °C. Compare as-cast HfMoTaTiZr baseline and modified compositions for density, microstructure, and mechanical response at 25 °C, 800 °C, and 1000 °C.
measurements: Tensile or compression strength at high temperatures up to 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Should any substituted alloy show >3% reduced strength at 1000 °C or exhibit substantial embrittlement compared to baseline HfMoTaTiZr, the hypothesis is falsified.

Microstructure and phase constitution

To verify this novel alloy design strategy, an industrial scale AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 ingot of ~2.5 kg in weight was prepared, as shown in Fig. 1a . The bulk AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 alloy exhibited an excellent castability with few casting defects, significantly differentiating with other bulk HEAs. The tensile test specimen was machined from the bulk alloy ingot and is shown in Fig. 1b . The cast microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 is shown in Fig. 2a . Even in such a bulk cast ingot, a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure characteristic of eutectic alloys was achieved. The inter-lamellar spacing was about 2 μm. The coupled grown two phases showed a clear compositional contrast, with the regions marked by A in Fig. 2b were rich in Co, Cr and Fe, while the regions marked by B were rich in Al and Ni (detailed compositional information given in Table 1 ). An enlarged microstructure given in Fig. 2c shows that dense nanoscale NiAl-rich precipitates (marked as B II ) occurred in the CoCrFe-rich region.
